A thorough analysis of this model reveals that it steers around the $S$-parameter crisis by adopting either an inherently positive $S$-parameter or one that can be made non-positive through a fine-tuned adjustment, accompanied by $H$ mass that can either mimic the LHC search patterns of the standard model Higgs boson or exhibit distinct characteristics. A companion public code is also made available to facilitate further calculations of this model's properties. To accomplish this, we'll draw on a large dataset of Wikipedia articles, incorporating both the summaries and full content of each entry. A key challenge arises from the diverse nature of Wikipedia articles, covering numerous subjects, styles, and lengths. To tackle this problem, we propose a multi-step generator network consisting of a summary generator and a long-form generator. The process begins with producing a summary of the target article's main points, using a dedicated generator network. This summary serves as input for the main generator network, which produces a complete text based on the initial summary. To further refine the generated text, we introduce a coherent self-consistency reward, a score system that assesses the similarity between the original article and the generated text. This self-consistency reward is calculated using a set of features extracting local and global structural characteristics from the articles. To handle the vast disparity in lengths between summaries and full articles, we've implemented a restart strategy for the generator network. This approach involves generating text in segments, merging them later to create the final article. To evaluate our generator network, we created a dataset of truncated Wikipedia summaries with corresponding full articles. This dataset allows us to use the coherence self-consistency reward as a benchmark to gauge the structural coherence of the generated text relative to the original article. This work extends the efficient and accurate full-orbital density-functional theory based on the adiabatic perturbation approach to include interactions and correlations, allowing for a direct analysis of fermionic correlations in time-dependent scenarios, including phonon-induced superconductivity and electron-electron scattering. Experimental signatures associated with these phenomena, including phonon-induced superconductivity and entanglement in transition metal complexes, are identified and it is proposed that further research into these effects is necessary to fully understand their potential for experimentation. However, the current understanding of how representations become ``useful'' is limited.  We propose an interpretable disentangled model where two separate networks, one for classification and one for constructing a feature space, are connected in series.  This design allows us to analyze the process of representation becoming ``useful''.  We found that a network can produce high-quality representations even when the input has no relation to the target, and the usefulness of a representation is directly related to its similarity to the network's internal codings, specifically the latent variables that encode disentangled features.  We demonstrated this theory's applicability to various tasks by manipulating the codings and observing the impact on performance.  This approach provides a detailed understanding of how representations become useful in artificial neural networks.  We also found that not all codings are equally important, and their individual impact can be measured by evaluating the information they contain about the task at hand.  This research can serve as a foundation for exploring more sophisticated methods to analyze and improve the quality of representations. A significant challenge in computational biology is to predict a protein's three-dimensional structure from its genetic sequence, and various methods have been developed to achieve this.  A key limitation of existing predictions is their lack of detail, as they typically represent a protein as a single average structure as opposed to a collection of distinct conformational states.  To address this, we've created an algorithm based on a Markovian mixture model that can predict multiple conformational states for a protein of known sequence, and we've applied this model to simulate the movement of an individual ribosome translating mRNA into a long peptide chain.  Experimental validation of our predicted conformational states for a ribosome shows that different parts of the chain occupy distinct positions, and we've found that the first part of the chain is delayed in its translation by about 40 amino acids, and it takes over 100 amino acids to reach a steady-state turnover.  Furthermore, our predicted states include a previously unrecognized conformational state for the ribosome, and we've found that different conformational states are associated with specific sections of the genetic code.  The accuracy of our predictions has been verified through multiple means, and we've found that different conformational states are linked to specific functional sites on the ribosome for factors such as eRF1 that read mRNA for stop codons.  The existence of conformational states on the ribosome provides a mechanism for how proteins with high sequence diversity can be encoded from a genetic template that is highly repetitive.  The underlying model for our predictions is a Markovian mixture model, and we've tested this model against multiple control models to verify its validity, and we believe that the conformational states of the ribosome with a phosphatidylserine headgroup are driven by an intrinsic stochastic fluctuation known as the "slippage" effect that occurs during translation. These patterns are not accounted for in conventional tensor manipulation techniques, leading to a need for an expanded framework that can handle these complex structures.  To that end, a new set of tools is being proposed to provide an augmented mathematical framework that reflects the inherent structure of these neural network modules, involving a combination of sparse, selective, and sequential operations, and incorporating a variety of embedding, pooling, and concatenation techniques.  This proposed framework can serve as a foundation for various applications, including automating tensor network creation, optimizing network parameters via gradient techniques, and incorporating external knowledge in the form of densely connected subnetworks.  An accompanying software package is also being provided to facilitate the exploration and utilization of this expanded framework in the form of a Python tensor environment that can be used with popular deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.  This environment supports a range of operations on tensors with unique structures and can be used to build a variety of networks, from image classification models involving convolutional layers to text classification models involving recurrent layers, along with many other applications.  Examples of networks that can be built using this environment include a convolutional neural network called ACNet that ranks 1st in efficiency among all deep neural networks, a recurrent neural network called ResER for relation extraction that ranks 1st in performance among all recurrent networks in the corresponding dataset, and many other successful networks in various datasets.  The proposed framework and associated Python environment are both highly customizable and efficient, making them valuable tools for building a wide range of neural networks that can be used in the training and evaluation of various models.  This approach has implications for fields like computer vision, natural language processing, and recommender systems, and the accompanying software package is available at a corresponding repository.  A supplementary documentation is also being provided that includes detailed implementation examples, a step-by-step tutorial on how to use the proposed framework, and a list of currently unsupported operations.  This documentation is highly useful for practitioners but is not included in the main text to facilitate a more streamlined presentation. This estimation method is designed to be highly efficient, with a linear cost in relation to the number of parameters, which is a significant improvement for large models. In standard Bayesian neural networks, the posterior distribution is characterized by the predictive variance, which is determined by the Hessian matrix of the log-likelihood function. However, calculating the Hessian explicitly is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we suggest using a first-order approximation of the Hessian, which is achieved by taking the weighted sum of the Hessian of the log-likelihood function and the gradient of the log-likelihood function multiplied by the output of the network. This estimation method is concise and permits the use of existing Bayesian neural network implementations as a starting point. We leverage this approximation to train a neural network using a Bayesian approach on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, with results showing that this technique yields a noticeable speed-up while maintaining a comparable level of accuracy. We also conducted additional experiments that evaluate the proposed method's scalability and found it to be highly efficient for large models. These results indicate that this technique is suitable for large-scale Bayesian neural networks. Given a positive integer $n$, we establish that equations of the form $x_1^p \cdot x_2^q \cdot... \cdot x_n^r = 1$ have at most $O(\epsilon, p, q, \ldots)$ solutions, where $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ are integers from a specified range, and $p, q, \ldots$ are fixed prime numbers except for possibly one variable with a bounded prime. Additionally, we demonstrate that for a given prime number $p$, the number of solutions to $a^p = 1$ is finite, and show that for any integer $a$ not equal to $0$ or $1$, the sequence $a, a^2, a^3, \ldots$ is relatively dense in the set of integers. A key argument in our proof utilizes the fact that for a prime number $p$, the group $({\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z})^*$ is cyclic, implying that the map $\phi: {\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z} \to {\mathbb Z}/p{\mathbb Z}$ defined by $\phi(a) = a^2$ is not injective, and thus has a non-trivial kernel, thereby giving us a bound for the number of solutions to $a^p = 1$. A related observation about the map $\phi$ leads to an application of Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions to a certain moduli space, resulting in a finite number of solutions for $a^p = 1$ and enabling us to extend our findings to equations involving a combination of perfect powers. A crucial observation about the growth of the sequence $a, a^2, a^3, \ldots$ enables us to establish the relative density of this sequence in the set of integers, which further enables us to extend our findings to a larger class of Diophantine equations involving perfect powers. A final example about the sequence $a, a^2, a^3, \ldots$ being relatively dense in the set of integers and its implications allows us to introduce the concept of relatively dense sequences and provide an informal argument on the implications of these sequences on the distribution of integers. A concluding remark about the current state and limitations of our findings, as well as possible directions for further research, are also presented.

  communications networks.  This report outlines our approach to developing a
  prototype for a low-bit-rate speech coder, which we call the Spectral Domain
  Code Exciter (SD-CEX).  This coder is modeled after the Code Exciter (CEX)
  algorithm but with a key modification, where the prediction and quantization
  processes are reversed.  Instead of using codebooks for speech prediction and
  excitation signal generation, we employ a different method, capturing the
  frequency-domain speech pattern and converting it into a binary stream.
  Analysis of our SD-CEX prototype reveals several key benefits, including
  simplified codebook training, increased robustness, and improved performance
  in terms of mean opinion score (MOS).  Specifically, we observed an MOS gain
  of 3.63 when using 10 codebooks per subband compared to 100 codebooks.
  Furthermore, our findings indicate that MOS scores obtained using the SD-CEX
  prototype and the original CEX algorithm converge when both use the same number
  of codebooks.  This indicates that the performance difference between the two
  algorithms is a result of codebook overfitting.  To prevent this, we propose
  increasing the distance between codebook vectors during training, which we
  found to be an effective solution.  This approach yields significant gains,
  with an MOS increase of 2.05 when using 10 codebooks per subband compared to
  100 codebooks.  This report presents our proposed speech coder framework,
  discusses the benefits and performance improvements resulting from reversing the
  prediction and quantization processes, and explores the phenomenon of codebook
  overfitting as well as potential solutions to address it.

ological implications of a newly proposed  Bartolomei-Bogoliubov theorem related to the energy spectrum of any Pauli-coupled two-body system. A general expression has been derived, showing that the energy spectrum can be determined from the eigenvalues of a specific matrix that depends on physical quantities, namely the reduced magnetic moment, electric dipole moment, and mass ratio. Consequently, the energy values can be expressed as weighted sums of these eigenvalues. A key outcome of the theorem is that the energy levels will exhibit the same relative spacing as the eigenvalues, thereby leading to a simplified interpretation of data. Furthermore, we demonstrate specific cases where the theorem applies to a system with a non-vanishing three-body force. A numerical analysis has been conducted to analyze the energy dependence of the eigenvalues and corresponding weight factors. This research confirms that the weighted sums can be accurately fit using a polynomial or arctangent function. The theorem has been particularly useful in analyzing data related to the $^{10}$B isoscalar decay channel, allowing for an extraction of the eigenvalue spectrum and subsequent interpretation of the results. Notably, we found that the eigenvalues exhibit a resonance pattern, providing a clear explanation for the earlier reported shape distortions. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the eigenvalues are much more sensitive to the meson-exchange three-body force than previously assumed, thereby advocating for a more comprehensive inclusion of such forces in nuclear physics calculations. A comparison has been made with existing calculations based on potential models, revealing that the energy spectrum derived from these models can be fit using the same functions as those obtained from the three-body force. The analysis also emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, as the latter is responsible for the resonance phenomenon. The results of this work suggest that future experiments aimed at extracting eigenvalues from measured energy spectra should be designed to identify the corresponding resonance pattern. The analysis of this work implies that the $^{10}$B experiment can be efficiently analyzed using a combined analysis of the magnetic and electric form factors in the $^{10}$B decay channel. The proposed experimental design for the $^{10}$B experiment involves measuring the energy spectrum of the decay products following the $^{10}$B reaction induced by a polarized neutron beam of a few MeV. The expected resolution of such a detector system is approximately 100 keV, which is sufficient to resolve the resonance pattern associated with the eigenvalues.   the internet, allowing for scalable infrastructure sharing. As the demand
  for cloud computing grows, potential users are cautious about choosing
  providers due to security and performance concerns. In multi-cloud scenarios,
  deciding between different providers becomes even more complex.
  Currently, evaluating cloud services involves manual testing and
  experimentation, which is time-consuming and inefficient. Existing
  benchmarking tools focus primarily on assessing performance, ignoring
  essential aspects like pricing, security, and support. Moreover, most
  benchmarks are static and cannot be easily adapted, making them
  ineffective for real-world applications. A scalable and actionable cloud
  benchmarking framework is necessary to efficiently evaluate cloud services
  and provide insights into their underlying costs. In this paper, we present
  Cibe, a cloud benchmarking framework that leverages programmable
  infrastructure to create dynamic and detailed reports of cloud service costs
  and performance. Validating Cibe shows it significantly outperforms
  existing benchmarking tools in terms of assessment speed and comprehensive
  data coverage. Additionally, we include a preliminary analysis of cloud cost
  functions to facilitate more precise and automated benchmark configuration. 
  This facilitates optimized cloud infrastructure deployment, thereby
  streamlining testing workflows. The framework and accompanying case study
  are available on GitHub at the specified link.

machine learning algorithm is supplied 
  with a subset of data and must make informed decisions about which remaining 
  information to acquire. This problem is particularly challenging for multi-class 
  classification, as it involves striking a balance between diverse data collection 
  and targeted, high-yield learning. This paper presents a novel approach, called 
  diverse and targeted (DaT), which employs a bipediated ranking system to 
  prioritize new data acquisition. On one hand, a diverse metric ensures that the 
  algorithm selects data that represents a broad range of existing classes, 
  preventing it from becoming too specialized. On the other hand, a targeted 
  component prioritizes data that is likely to result in an accurate classification, 
  either by mirroring existing class distribution or by focusing on under-represented 
  categories. This system can be further optimized by adjusting parameters that 
  control the balance between diversity, targeted selection, and overall classification 
  performance. Experimental results demonstrate the advantages of DaT in both 
  fully- and partially-labeled settings. As an illustration of the algorithm's 
  versatility, we show that DaT can be applied to a range of classification tasks, 
  including those with varying numbers of classes and sample sizes. As the algorithm 
  is designed to handle multi-class classification, we also highlight its capability 
  to scale to large numbers of classes with minimal parameter adjustments. As an 
  example, we demonstrate DaT's effectiveness on a dataset consisting of 100 classes 
  and show that with a simple parameter tuning, it is possible to achieve nearly 
  double the accuracy compared to a standard active learning approach. As an 
  extension of the algorithm, we also present a variant called diverse and targeted 
  with noise (DaT-N), which is specifically designed to handle noisy data. As an 
  example, we demonstrate DaT-N's capability to scale to large datasets consisting 
  of 1000 samples with a significant proportion (25\%) of noisy data and show that 
  it is possible to achieve accuracy well above chance level even when the majority 
  of the data is deemed irrelevant. As an indication of the algorithm's potential 
  applications, we also present results on DaT-N's capability to select diverse and 
  targeted data when the algorithm is supplied with a constraint on the size of the 
  sample, as well as results on DaT-N's capability to achieve high accuracy when 
  the algorithm is supplied with a constraint on the threshold

This paper focuses on an extension of this concept, exploring the characteristics of functions that result from the solution of a generalized Riemann-Hilbert problem. It demonstrates that functions produced by a generalized Riemann-Hilbert problem will always exhibit one of two behaviors: their growth will either remain within established limits or, under certain conditions, they will exhibit an exponentially high degree of complexity. This paper also investigates the fundamental condition that gives rise to this latter phenomenon, offering an inequality that any such family of functions must satisfy in order to exhibit this behavior, and provides an intuitive explanation for this inequality's significance. Furthermore, this paper presents a specific example of a family of functions that meets this condition, thereby exhibiting an otherwise generally observed pattern, and provides a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between the Riemann-Hilbert problem and the Bieberbach conjecture, a result that was previously established by other mathematicians. This framework demonstrates that any family of functions that contravenes the inequality will have a subfamily whose growth exceeds established limits at a specific rate, and also establishes that the growth of functions produced by a generalized Riemann-Hilbert problem is directly tied to the value of a specific coefficient that appears in growth-related equations. This coefficient is in turn tied to another coefficient that appears in growth-related equations and, when set to a specific value, ensures that functions meet specific growth requirements, including those required by the Riemann-Hilbert problem and the Bieberbach conjecture. This paper also explores the implications of growing functions on the space of analytic functions and the associated transform, providing insights into the nature of functions that result from the solution of a generalized Riemann-Hilbert problem. This paper also introduces a new inequality that any family of functions must satisfy in order to meet certain growth requirements, and demonstrates the applicability of this inequality to known families of functions, including families defined by growth-related equations such as the Carathéodory, Grunsky, and Neumann equations. This paper also presents a more general form of this inequality, providing it as a condition under which the growth of functions produced by a generalized Riemann-Hilbert problem will remain within established limits.   benefit being that INT models serve as a unified framework for various 
  latent space methods. During training, INT models optimize two objectives: 
  one that matches the posterior with the prior on the latent space, and 
  another that respects the original encoding process. We show that our proposed

  the original COPA model to incorporate encoding invariance,

An emerging bottom-up, agent-based approach provides a more precise method of calculating DERs' feed-in values and better system reliability, but it requires significant computational resources and can be challenging to model. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel two-tier power flow estimation framework for small-scale microgrids. This proposed framework, which is robust and efficient, utilizes a simplified top-down method for initial estimation and a bottom-up adjustment to ensure accuracy. This approach can be applied to various types of microgrids, including those with renewable energy sources, energy storage systems, and loads with time-varying profiles. The results of case studies demonstrate that the proposed framework accurately reflects real-world power flow conditions, crediting DERs' feed-in values correctly and providing valuable insights for microgrid management. This framework has been tested on multiple scenarios and meets the requirements of low computational complexity, making it suitable for real-time applications. The proposed algorithm's linear time complexity ensures that it can be applied to complex systems without sacrificing accuracy, giving it immense value for widespread microgrid management technology implementation. -based approximation to the solution of a time-independent Schr\"{o}dinger equation with a periodic potential, with the aim of elucidating the relationship between potential smoothness and the asymptotic behavior of the solution's high-frequency Fourier mode coefficients. We demonstrate that when the potential is smooth, the sum of the square roots of the high-frequency mode coefficients converges to a non-negative constant as the mode frequency tends to infinity. The proof involves a combination of a diagonalization scheme for the Hamiltonian, an operator theoretic analysis of the imaginary part of the complex-valued spectral density of the Hamiltonian, and a application of the Wiener Integral to the imaginary part of the complex-valued spectral density of a model operator. This results in a significant extension of a previous finding to the case of smooth rather than just continuous potentials. Furthermore, we also show that this constant can be expressed in terms of a measure that is derived from the complex-valued spectral density of the Hamiltonian and characterize this measure in the model case. This research is a culmination of earlier partial results and involves multiple new insights. The proposed proof approach can be applied to a broad class of operators that are referred to as quasi-Hermitian operators. The asymptotic behavior of the sum of the square roots of the high-frequency mode coefficients is known to be related to the fractal dimension of the underlying potential and can be characterized in terms of the scaling properties of this dimension. One-area evaluation, representing a paradigm for evaluating models on a single task, is a widely accepted and straightforward approach.  However, it doesn't account for real-world scenarios where models are often  required to perform well on a variety of tasks after gaining new  experiences. In such multi-task scenarios, relying solely on single-task evaluation can be misleading and leads to biased performance  recommendations when safe and efficient machine learning applications are  considered. These applications prioritize robust generalization and accurate  uncertainty estimation to prevent catastrophic failures and minimize  expensive re-training when models are deployed in practice. Current neural network optimization techniques, which employ gradient descent, take an inordinate number of trials to explore all possible architectures and train corresponding networks until convergence. To tackle this challenge, our novel algorithm, called Efficient Architecture Selection (EAS), is developed. EAS employs a controlling network that generates a set of discrete control tokens, which in turn determine architecture hyperparameters. A controlling network encoder is trained to produce an embedding of these control tokens, and this process is encapsulated within a controller network module. The controller network module is integrated into the one-shot architecture search framework, which searches for the best architecture based on performance. To ensure the purity of the sampled architecture, our fairness-inducing technique is proposed, which balances the controller network to avoid overfitting to minority classes. Experimental results show that EAS achieves remarkable performance on multiple datasets when evaluated on a wide range of architecture search tasks. The proposed technique demonstrates substantial improvements over current optimization techniques and rivals the state-of-the-art architecture search methods in terms of accuracy. The underlying mechanism of EAS is also thoroughly examined through additional experiments, which show that discretization losses are minimal and the controller network is capable of generalizing across different datasets. While there are numerous datasets available for other classification tasks, a large, accurately labeled dataset for offensive language detection is hard to find.  To address this gap, we present a new dataset called "Hate Speech Data Set" (HSDS) that comprises over 10,000 English utterances, labeled as either non-offensive or hateful.  This dataset stands out from other existing datasets in several ways.  Firstly, its size is unparalleled among current hate speech datasets.  Secondly, its categorization system is more refined, distinguishing between mild and severe hate speech.  Lastly, its development process involved multiple annotation iterations to enhance the accuracy of its labels.  To evaluate the effectiveness of HSDS, we conducted several experiments using machine learning models.  These experiments demonstrated that models trained on smaller, commonly used datasets often spread hate speech during deployment.  In contrast, models trained on HSDS consistently reduced hate speech propagation.  To make HSDS accessible for further research, we've incorporated it into the Hatemoji Dataset Repository.  Additionally, we've created a companion dataset called "Hate Speech Data Set: Refined" (HSDR) that includes only the most severe hate speech from HSDS, making it an efficient tool for model fine-tuning in tasks like zero-shot transfer learning.  Our findings also imply that using smaller datasets can lead to the propagation of hate speech on social media platforms, emphasizing the necessity of using large, accurately labeled datasets for effective model training.  To accelerate progress in this domain, we're offering rewards for further annotations of HSDR and invite researchers to participate in the hate speech detection community.  Finally, we've made both HSDS and HSDR available on the Hateful Memes Challenge GitHub page for public use.  We believe that HSDS and HSDR will serve as invaluable resources for developing more effective models to combat hate speech in social media platforms.  We're also excited to share the results of this research at the IEEE ICME 2021 conference during the workshop titled "Artificial Intelligence for Multimedia 2021".  We hope that this research and associated datasets will contribute to the creation of more accurate models to identify and prevent the dissemination of hate speech on social media platforms.  We're confident that, together with the research community, we can develop more reliable solutions to address this critical challenge

This limitation makes them less suitable for embedded systems with limited memory and power constraints. This problem motivates the development of compact graph neural networks that prioritize efficiency without sacrificing effectiveness. In this paper, a novel architecture called multi-path reduced neural network (MPRNN) is presented, which yields both significant reductions in model size and computational requirements. Unlike previous optimization strategies focused solely on model compression, MPRNN addresses both width and depth in a unified framework. Specifically, the network divides the classification task into multiple distinct path classifications, then combines these classifications via reduced neural networks. This design allows for trade-offs between model size, computational requirements, and classification accuracy. Experimental evaluations on multiple graph datasets demonstrate that MPRNN achieves performance on par with large models, surpasses several compression baselines in both model size and computational efficiency, and exhibits a wide range of depth vs. width adaptability. A case study showcasing MPRNN's applicability on an embedded system illustrates its suitability for resource-constrained devices. This paper's results provide a useful reference for developing compact graph neural networks in various industries. Code for MPRNN is available at https://github.com/zyeng1990/MPRNN. Yet, the standard way to model these phenomena relies on continuous mathematical tools, despite the inherently discrete nature of the processes in question.  This research proposes a novel mathematical framework based on difference equations to analyze binary state transitions, with a key insight being the identification of an equivalent system of equations where the variables are transformed to represent the underlying probabilistic processes.  By applying this formulation, we can demonstrate how the (often complicated) behavior of binary state transitions can be interpreted using the concepts of fixed points, stability, and bifurcations that are typical of classical dynamical systems.  As a concrete example, we explore the dynamics of a specific difference equation and show how its binary state transitions can be predicted by solving a related map, with the condition for this method's applicability being the equation's mean field property.  Furthermore, we demonstrate how this formulation can be utilized to investigate the relationships between the parameters that define these processes, with a resulting map that can be studied for its fixed points, stability, and bifurcations.  This research is accompanied by numerical and analytical studies of a non-trivial difference equation representing a paradigmatic model of binary state transitions, with a key finding being the existence of multiple stable points for certain values of the model's parameter.  The predictions derived from this formulation were compared to the results obtained through a Monte Carlo simulation with a large number of samples, with the agreement between the two indicating the reliability of the proposed mathematical framework.  This research provides a suitable example where the standard model's known results can be recovered, in addition to revealing additional insights that were difficult to obtain.  The key aspects of this research can be applied to a broader class of difference equations that exhibit the mean field property, with a notable exception being equations with a non-constant birth rate where the underlying process is not completely specified.  In such cases, a partial analytical solution can be obtained, but further progress requires additional specifications of the underlying process.  This research is complemented by an accompanying code that enables readers to directly access and execute numerical and analytical studies similar to the ones presented here.  This code can serve as a model for readers to apply the same methods to other difference equations.  The key insights obtained from this research can be summarized as a set of theorems that define the conditions under which the difference equations exhibit binary state transitions, with a related map that can be studied for its fixed points, stability, and bifurcations.

Notably, this proposal offers a means to replicate complex lattice thermodynamic phenomena on multiple, closely spaced nitrogen-vacancy centers using a single laser configuration. In this context, attributed event sequences represent events linked by causality or temporal relationships, along with associated attributes or features.  Event sequence classification is a fundamental task that has been extensively studied, but the classification of complex structured data, such as trees, has received relatively little attention.  We introduce a novel deep learning framework called TimelyNodeNetwork (TNN) to address this challenge.  TNN treats the attributed event sequence as a directed tree, where each node represents an event with its features and a classification label.  This model leverages a two-part mechanism where the node classifier prioritizes the most relevant events to consider, and then the node aggregator determines the optimal timing for each event to be considered.  This is achieved through a linear decay function along the causality graph.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of TNN through comparative experiments on multiple datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing methods.  Additionally, TNN's ability to generate an interpretable causality graph provides valuable insights for domain experts.  We further analyze the advantages of TNN's temporal attention mechanism and the fixed-point decay strategy, highlighting the importance of both mechanisms in the comparative experiment results.  We conclude by highlighting potential applications and areas for further development of the TimelyNodeNetwork framework. Our findings show that both novice and experienced programmers find it difficult to grasp the concept of partial functions, although they struggle in distinct ways. application in Natural Language Processing (NLP).  The development of large-scale machine translation systems has been hindered by the lack of labeled data in many scenarios.  This challenge is particularly pronounced in low-resource languages.  The emergence of few-shot learning has provided a potential solution to tackle such problems.  Initially designed for vision and language tasks, existing few-shot learning methods are not directly applicable to character-level machine translation systems.  These systems require a different approach, considering that the model's character-level predictions are categorical in nature.  To address this, a new few-shot learning model called FSLCT has been proposed, incorporating a functional neural network to capture the relationship between input sequences and output probability distributions.  This model leverages the notion of subsequence functions to analyze the underlying structure of small datasets.  Through experiments on 14 low-resource languages, FSLCT has shown notable improvements over the baseline char2char model, achieving higher BLEU scores and smaller character error rates.  Additionally, a comparison with a comparable TTS-based char2char model has confirmed its superiority.  An analysis of FSLCT's working mechanism has been conducted, showcasing the effectiveness of its designed components.  Further modifications to FSLCT have led to the derivation of a head-to-head few-shot learning char2char model, also exhibiting notable char ER and BLEU score improvements.  An evaluation of FSLCT's current limitations and potential areas for enhancement has been presented, including the exploration of integrating more explicit character dependencies and the use of more nuanced few-shot learning techniques.  A code release for FSLCT has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/MXL2022-FSLCT.  Experimental evidence has demonstrated that FSLCT's working mechanism is marked by a marked decrease in the difficulty of adapting to new languages following the initial transition.  To account for this phenomenon, a new metric called the difficulty of zero-shot character adaptation has been proposed, correlating with the behavior of FSLCT and facilitating further research into the underlying mechanics.  An analysis of this metric has involved an integrated evaluation of FSLCT's working mechanism, encompassing results from 14 low-resource language datasets.  This evaluation has been conducted by creating additional difficult zero-shot character adaptation datasets, obtained through the manipulation of existing datasets based on character sets, grammar, and vocabulary.  These newly constructed difficult zero-shot character adaptation datasets have been used to train and evaluate FSLCT, exhibiting a marked improvement in its performance.   SDN is the ability to rapidly implement new network protocols and test  
  them on real networks. However, traditional SDN testbeds have a major  
  limitation in that they are typically built using commodity hardware  
  devices that adhere strictly to the IEEE 802.3 Ethernet standard,  
  limiting the scope of protocols that can be tested on them. For  
  instance, devices that use Ethernet cannot route packets with different  
  MAC addresses as the destination. Moreover, they cannot forward packets  
  based on their logical or semantic properties, a capability essential  
  for protocols like hierarchical link awareness. Consequently, a scalable  
  and flexible SDN testbed is necessary that can support a broad range  
  of protocols by leveraging a more universal and higher-level network  
  technology - IPv4. Our research introduces Riviera, a high-speed IPv4-  
  based SDN testbed designed to evaluate new network protocols in real-  
  time environments. Riviera is built using low-cost, high-performance  
  hardware devices that support routing, switching, and forwarding functions  
  at layer 3, thus enabling devices to direct packets based on their  
  destination IP addresses. As a result, Riviera can support a wide range  
  of protocols, including hierarchical link awareness, provides a suitable  
  platform for quickly deploying and testing software-defined network  
  protocols, and offers a flexible and manageable network environment.  
  Our experiments show that Riviera offers significant improvements in  
  forwarding throughput, packet forwarding delay, and switch overhead  
  compared to traditional Ethernet-based testbeds, indicating that it is  
  suitable for evaluating protocols that prioritize efficient IP forwarding.  
  In addition, Riviera provides a reliable and scalable solution for  
  testing protocol hierarchies, reduces test deployment time, and  
  provides multiple network topology options. Consequently, Riviera is  
  particularly well-suited for use in software-defined network protocol  
  testing, protocol development, protocol optimization, protocol  
  experimentation, and educational purposes.

We demonstrate that any instance with extensive misrepresentation cannot support a truthful mechanism for determining an stable matching, thereby illustrating the importance of this instance characteristic.  Furthermore, we show that instances with modest versions of this property, though uncommon, are still crucial in certain scenarios.  Specifically, we find that they are necessary for addressing several challenging problems in SP theory.  Additionally, we identify a boundary between instances with little and those with significant misrepresentation, demonstrating that this boundary is computationally decidible, albeit with a high time complexity of $2^{O(n^{\epsilon})}$ for any $\epsilon > 0$, and showing that this is a significant limitation by achieving a lower bound when $\epsilon$ is an arbitrarily small positive number.  Notably, this decision complexity can be greatly simplified to $O(1)$ when restricted to instances where, for any stable matching, the majority of agents have a single preferred swap.  We also demonstrate that this decision problem is reducible to a version of the weak exponential time hypothesis (WETH) and present a preliminary analysis of this connection.  We also demonstrate that instances with extensive misrepresentation are rare by establishing a bound on the number of possible orders of agent preferences of $n^{\omega(\log\log n)}$ for any $\omega > 0$, albeit this result is shown to be an exaggeration as we can achieve a growth rate of $n^{\log\log n}$, and present an informal argument for this fact.  We also demonstrate that this growth rate is necessary by establishing a family of instances with extensive misrepresentation of growth rate $n^{\log\log n}$.  We also demonstrate that this decision problem is solvable for a specific class of instances with extensive misrepresentation in a time complexity of $O(n^{\log\log n})$, and present an informal argument for this result.  We also demonstrate that this decision problem is reducible to a version of the WETH, and present an informal argument for this connection.  We also propose and examine a static approximation algorithm for determining whether an instance has extensive misrepresentation, and present an analysis of this algorithm.  We also propose and examine a natural characteristic of instance classes with extensive misrepresentation, and present an informal argument for this characteristic.

We demonstrate that all geodesics eventually become classified into one of two main categories: those that remain a finite distance apart from a single straight line, and those that eventually split into multiple paths. We also analyze the way geodesics interact with the space's boundary, including its outer boundary and any internal boundaries. We show that the way geodesics behave at the boundary is determined by a set of simple, applicable criteria. We then explore the possibility of geodesics splitting into multiple paths in more detail, including the time it takes for this to happen and the distance between the resulting paths. A new challenge is therefore described that focuses on the empirical analysis of NLP models via truthful question posing, using a carefully constructed set of 13 challenges based on diverse, previously established datasets. directionally-coupled oscillations for the diagnosis of mechanical anomalies, research focuses on identifying defective components through the coupling effects that give rise to prominent resonant peaks in frequency-response curves.  However, the impact of directional coupling on frequency-response curves is highly sensitive to excitation direction, posing a significant challenge for its effective utilization.  This study investigates the coupling effects that give rise to resonant peaks in frequency-response curves along principal and intermediate directions of coupling.  It shows that the location, magnitude, and shape of these peaks can change dramatically with even a small adjustment of the excitation direction.  Consequently, various methods that accurately capture the direction of the excitation inertia tensor are crucial for accurately interpreting frequency-response curves.  To this end, a step-by-step procedure is developed to analyze the curvature of frequency-response curves along a given path, which helps in identifying the direction of maximum curvature and thereby the direction of the smallest eigenvalue of the inertia tensor.  This information is then incorporated into a surrogate-assisted optimization algorithm to rapidly determine the direction of minimal resonance and the associated delay time, frequency of the peak, and peak amplitude.  This proposed framework can be applied to and evaluated on a faulty timing belt drive system, which indicates that it can effectively diagnose directional-coupled oscillations even when the excitation direction is unknown, reducing the computational cost by up to 7 times and accurately predicting the peak frequency and amplitude with a root mean square error of 0.05 and 0.23, respectively.  This study confirms that frequency-response curves exhibit directional variability with even a small adjustment of the excitation direction.  To overcome this challenge, a surrogate-assisted optimization algorithm is developed to rapidly determine the direction of minimal resonance and the associated physical parameters for a faulty timing belt drive system.  This algorithm can significantly reduce the computational cost and is applicable to and evaluatable on real-world systems.  However, further research is necessary to develop more robust and physically-meaningful methods to analyze the curvature of frequency-response curves and to investigate the applicability of the proposed algorithm to other types of directional-coupled oscillations.  Additionally, the development of detection and diagnosis algorithms for anomalies in systems with directional-coupled oscillations is lagging behind compared to the analysis of these oscillations, hence, more attention should be paid to this aspect in the future. This loop is known as the Hamiltonian circuit length or Hamiltonian distance. The Hamiltonian circuit length of a graph can be determined using a variant of Dijkstra's algorithm, and we show that this process can be optimized to run in $O(n^2 \log n)$ time on a grid graph, with a specific application to the $n\times n$ grid showing a solution of $O(n^2 \log n)$ time complexity for this problem. While cognitive scientists propose that neural networks benefit from being trained on multiple languages due to their inherent ability to capture linguistic patterns and concepts, others suggest a more practical explanation related to model scaling. In this study, we investigate the impact of training multilingual models on high-frequency words in a single language by exploring three variations: removing bigram frequency information, incorporating dictionary-based knowledge, and utilizing weighted character embedding. Our experiments reveal that introducing weighted character embedding leads to improved results, exceeding the effectiveness of training multilingual models on diverse languages. This finding suggests that the benefits of multilingual training can be largely attributed to capturing frequent language patterns rather than linguistic and cognitive aspects. To further analyze this, we developed an all-English model that incorporates weighted character embedding and saw significant improvements in performance. This new model is now an attractive baseline to consider for future English-only machine translation systems.  We also found that character weighting is particularly beneficial for modeling the high-frequency words found in speech, internet, and telephony dialogues. Moreover, the importance of character weighting decreases as we move to model more rare words, supporting the frequency-based hypothesis.   objects within falsified images.  Encouraging progress has been made using
  Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), yet significant improvements are still needed
  for the technique to be practical for widespread use.  DNNs, particularly
  codetection algorithms, often struggle with partially obscured objects
  since these objects contravene the unique object assumption underlying
  conventional object detection methods.  This assumption stipulates that
  individual detection boxes contain a single, unobstructed object. 
  Codetection algorithms have historically been ineffective at processing
  partially hidden objects.  This research introduces a novel codetection
  model called Spatially-Aware Codetection Network (SACNet).  SACNet addresses
  codetection challenges posed by partially obscured objects by integrating a
  simple prior into its training regimen that encourages multiple targets
  within a single detection box.  This allows the model to effectively
  prioritize the detection of codetections even when objects overlap. 
  Evaluations using the COD-50 dataset reveal that SACNet achieves notable
  performance gains compared to current state-of-the-art codetection algorithms
  for both unmodified and artificially created overlapping scenarios. 
  Furthermore, SACNet performs comparably to models trained on dense annotation
  sets even though it was trained on a sparse codetection dataset. 
  Encouragingly, SACNet shows significant improvement in codetection precision
  at the 0.5 IOU threshold, indicating that it detects complete targets
  effectively when partial targets are marked during annotation. 
  Additionally, SACNet's evaluation on the codetection part of the Security
  Automatic Check System (SACS) dataset reveals that it achieves a mean AP
  (mAP) of 33.9% at the 0.5 IOU threshold, indicating that it has practical
  value in real-world applications. 
  To explore the generalizability of SACNet, a variant was trained and tested
  on codetection datasets from unrelated domains (e.g., traffic light detection
  on ImageNet Light) with results showing that it performs well. 
  Finally, an analysis of the codetection distribution of SACNet highlights
  its ability to prioritize codetections even when objects are not actually
  present, suggesting that it overdetects codetections to some extent. 
  This encourages further research into codetection quality control. 
  Code and models for SACNet are available at https://github.com
